title: Demand Paging: When the Page Isn't in RAM
topic: Demand paging — virtual pages live on disk and are loaded into physical frames only when touched. The present bit, the page-fault trap, the swap-in animation, and what happens when RAM is full and a victim must be evicted first.

beats.narration: Your program thinks it owns gigabytes of memory. In reality, only the pages you actively touch live in RAM. The rest sit on disk until you need them.

elements.content: RAM is small. Programs can be much bigger.

beats.narration: Physical memory holds a handful of page frames. The disk swap area holds many more. The present bit in each page-table entry says which store to look in.

elements.content: RAM = fast, small · DISK = slow, big
RAM block (4 frame slots, two filled with V1 and V3) at top; disk block below (many pages V0, V2, V4...). Page-table column shows present=1/0 next to each virtual page

beats.narration: When the CPU reads a virtual page whose present bit is zero, the hardware traps into the kernel. The page-fault handler finds the page on disk and copies it into a free frame. Then the access can be retried.

elements.content: CPU requests V2; page-table row pulses (present=0) → trap glyph → page tile V2 slides up from disk slot into the free RAM frame; present bit flips to 1

beats.narration: If RAM is already full, one of the resident pages has to leave first. The replacement policy picks a victim, writes it back if dirty, and only then the new page can land.

elements.content: RAM full → evict before bringing in
Old victim page V1 slides DOWN from RAM back to disk; then new page V5 slides UP into the now-free frame

beats.narration: Hit in RAM, it's nanoseconds. Miss to disk, it's milliseconds. Demand paging only pays that price for what you actually use.

elements.content: five orders of magnitude — keep your working set small
